subtitle: Equity in program evaluation begins with a useful question. This course helps you read responses faithfully, staying true to what people said, and build a well-supported next line of inquiry.
scope: For staff and leaders across DHS. All people, demonstration responses and comparisons are original example. Thirty unique invented attendees are invited once by email after one demonstration; eighteen answer once, twelve affirm next-step understanding and six are uncertain. Twelve invitees have no supplied answer. Reported understanding is not observed application or a whole-program result. A separate hypothetical twenty-person comparison illustrates causal limits, not later survey observations or demographic groups. Willa’s learning-circle encounter and Alden’s allegation example are distinct. The Equity and Inclusion Operations Consultant leads the program and provides guidance, knowledge and feedback while staff carry their own equity work. Actual information and decision duties remain. Native American- and Tribal-specific matters remain referral-only to the person or area responsible within ADSA.
introTranscript: Follow Zora and Felix as they choose a fitting question, explain the demonstration responses and separate a descriptive comparison from a causal claim. Consider personally offered meanings of a useful result and retain actual responsibilities. Return a clear finding and justified next inquiry without inventing approval, action or later effects.

lessons.title: Choose a question that the evidence can answer
lessons.summary: Start with a specific purpose and keep a reported understanding separate from a complete program result.
lessons.objective: Define the question answered by the practice demonstration survey.
objectives: Define the question answered by the practice demonstration survey.
Distinguish reported next-step understanding from completed action or program impact.
Identify who is outside the supplied invitation and response sets.
takeaways: The evaluation question gives the findings their meaning.
A reported understanding is not a verified action or benefit.
An invitation list does not automatically represent everyone a program serves.
lessons.statement: A useful evaluation begins with a clear question and an honest description of whose experience it includes.

image.caption: Four people lean toward one another and stack their hands above a table with papers, cups and laptops.

intro.heading: Choose a question that the evidence can answer
intro.body:
Zora and Felix are discussing an original practice demonstration about choosing a next action when reviewing a work process. Thirty unique invented attendees were invited once by email to answer a short question after that one demonstration. Eighteen responded once. Twelve selected “I could identify the next step,” and six selected “I am not yet sure which action fits.” Twelve invitees did not respond. The course supplies those figures and response choices, not the demonstration materials, actual staff records or an assessment of every DHS program.

Felix initially describes the exercise as an evaluation of whether the whole program works. Zora asks what the response choices can establish. They concern whether respondents said they could identify a next step after a particular demonstration. They do not show whether anyone took that step, whether it was correct for a real situation, whether a process changed or whether the change helped people. The narrower question is still useful. It makes room to examine what the demonstration helped respondents understand and where questions may remain without announcing a larger result.

The question and the people included must be described together. The thirty invitees are the supplied attendees, not all staff who might use a resource. People who did not attend, did not receive this invitation or might use another form of learning are not described by these figures. The exercise provides no reason for their absence, no count of them and no permission to obtain their information. A broad claim about all staff would need an appropriately designed inquiry and evidence for that claim. It cannot be created by changing the heading above these particular responses.

Zora also separates what the evaluators know from what they want to learn. The supplied affirmative response is a self-report about identifying a step. It is not an independently observed demonstration of skill. The uncertain response identifies an unresolved question for those six respondents; it does not prove that the learning was useless or that those people lack capability. The other twelve invitees remain unknown on the question because their answers are not supplied. No one’s commitment, cultural perspective or intercultural development level can be assigned from the response choice or absence of a response.

Program evaluation can use different questions and methods for different purposes. The CDC framework offers a flexible approach to understanding context, choosing questions, gathering credible evidence, drawing supported conclusions and acting on learning. It is not a requirement to apply one survey or one denominator to every activity. A question about access to learning may need different evidence from a question about a policy’s effects. Relevant perspectives and actual responsibilities help decide what fits.

Privately write the narrower purpose in your own words: understand the supplied respondents’ reported next-step understanding after one practice demonstration. Then name the larger questions left open. The value of this first step is a question that can guide thoughtful inquiry, rather than an impressive label that asks the evidence to answer something it never measured.

accordion.heading: Examine the question and its consequences

items.title: Retain the question the choices support
items.body: The affirmative choice concerns identifying a next step. Calling it proof of effective policy implementation would enlarge the event. Zora can keep the response useful by stating what was asked and separating a possible later question about applying that step. No demonstrated application is supplied. The consequence is a credible starting inquiry rather than a claim about changes the demonstration has not been shown to cause.

items.title: Describe the people actually included
items.body: The thirty invitees attended this practice demonstration. Neither the invitation list nor eighteen responses is a complete account of everyone who might use the program. Felix can name that limit without treating all other staff as disengaged. The question of broader access remains available for a fitting inquiry; it cannot be answered through an invented count or unauthorized search for absent people.

items.title: Keep uncertainty meaningful
items.body: Six respondents were not yet sure which action fit. That is an answer with a distinct meaning, not the same as twelve invitees whose answers are absent. A useful follow-up question might explore what remained unclear. The supplied figures do not explain the uncertainty or prove that a particular change would resolve it. Keeping those distinctions supports inquiry without diagnosing individual capability.

tabs.heading: Compare the interpretation and next inquiry

tabs.label: A response becomes program success
tabs.body: Felix writes that the demonstration proved the program effective because twelve respondents could identify a step. The finding is narrower and self-reported. Zora changes the conclusion to describe the selected response and identifies action and broader effects as unanswered questions. This preserves useful information while refusing an unsupported claim of completed improvement.

tabs.label: An invitation becomes universal coverage
tabs.body: Zora initially labels the thirty attendees all staff reached by the program. The example describes no such population definition. Felix identifies the actual invitation set and notes that other potential learners are not described. They can consider an access question, but the practice invitation list gives no authority to locate or classify people outside it.

tabs.label: The purpose matches the evidence
tabs.body: Felix describes an inquiry into reported next-step understanding among the respondents after one practice demonstration. Zora retains the uncertain and absent answers separately and names application and wider access as open questions. The conclusion is limited but useful. It does not claim a complete evaluation of the program or personal development.

check.question: What question do the supplied response choices most directly address?
check.correct: Whether respondents reported being able to identify a next step after one practice demonstration.
wrong: Whether every DHS employee can apply equity analysis independently.
Whether the program caused a lasting improvement in services.
Whether nonrespondents oppose the program’s purpose.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. This question stays within the supplied response choices, people and occasion.
check.feedbackIncorrect: The case does not describe every DHS employee or demonstrate independent application. No lasting service effects or causal comparison are supplied. An absent answer provides no evidence of opposition.

sorting.heading: Keep findings, questions and conclusions distinct

items.text: Thirty unique invented attendees were invited once by email.
Eighteen invitees responded once after one demonstration.
Did respondents later apply a correct next step?
Who outside the attendees could access suitable learning?
The survey proves the whole program works.
An absent response establishes opposition.

lessons.next: Continue to read the answers and the missing answers separately.

scenario.context: This example: Felix wants to use the demonstration responses as proof of the whole program’s effectiveness. No actual learning materials, later actions or service results are supplied.
scenario.prompt: How should Zora frame the inquiry?
options: Describe the supplied reported understanding, identify who answered and keep application and wider effects open.
Treat every affirmative response as a verified improvement in services.
Assign disengagement to all invitees who did not answer.
responses: This produces a fitting question without dismissing the useful responses or enlarging them into unsupported outcomes.
Identifying a step in a response does not establish a later service result.
The absent answers contain no information about motivation.

lessons.transfer: Privately state the question, people and occasion covered by this inquiry, then identify one wider question it leaves open.

move.control: You can choose an evaluation question and describe the evidence’s actual reach.
move.failure: A narrow response becomes proof of whole-program effectiveness or a judgment about people.
move.next: Privately state the question, people and occasion covered by this inquiry, then identify one wider question it leaves open.

lessons.title: Read the answers and the missing answers separately
lessons.summary: Calculate a respondent finding and response coverage without turning unanswered invitations into success or failure.
lessons.objective: Calculate the affirmative percentage among the eighteen sample respondents.
objectives: Calculate the affirmative percentage among the eighteen sample respondents.
Calculate invitation response coverage and the recorded affirmative share of invitees.
Explain why nonresponse prevents a conclusion about all invitees’ understanding.
takeaways: An uncertain answer and an absent answer are not interchangeable.
A response percentage does not by itself establish representativeness.
lessons.statement: Keep the meaning of each count visible when presenting a percentage.

image.caption: Four people lean toward one another and stack their hands above a table with papers, cups and laptops.

intro.heading: Read the answers and the missing answers separately
intro.body:
The practice invitation set has thirty unique attendees. Eighteen responded once. Twelve of those eighteen selected “I could identify the next step,” and six selected “I am not yet sure which action fits.” Twelve invitees did not answer. Zora and Felix can calculate several accurate percentages, but they need to explain which question each answers. A correct calculation with the wrong description can still mislead.

Twelve affirmative responses divided by eighteen responses is approximately 66.7 percent. That describes the affirmative share among respondents. It does not establish the share of all thirty invitees who could identify a next step because twelve invitees have no supplied answer. Eighteen responses divided by thirty invitations is 60 percent. That describes response coverage for this exercise. It is not an understanding score or proof that the respondents represent the invitees who did not respond.

Twelve affirmative responses divided by thirty invitees is 40 percent. This is the recorded affirmative share of the invitation set. It should be described exactly that way, rather than reported as a 40 percent success rate or a 60 percent failure rate. Six invitees gave an uncertain answer, while twelve invitees gave no supplied answer. Those two sets do not have the same status. A person who says they are not yet sure has contributed information; an absent answer leaves their experience unknown. Neither establishes a lack of effort, a developmental orientation or a need for a prescribed personnel action.

Felix wants one number for a short presentation. Zora explains why the respondent finding needs response coverage beside it. Reporting only 66.7 percent could leave readers imagining that everyone invited answered. Reporting only 40 percent could make the absent answers look like negative answers. The pair can state the counts in a compact sentence: twelve of eighteen respondents, approximately 66.7 percent, selected the affirmative choice; eighteen of thirty invitees answered, 60 percent. Six respondents were uncertain, and twelve invitees’ answers remain unknown.

The exercise does not supply the reason for nonresponse. Timing, invitation delivery, relevance, accessibility or many other conditions might matter in an actual inquiry, but none is established here. An additional response route could be worth considering with affected people and appropriate roles. It would not automatically make a sample representative or prove that the invitation was inaccessible. Do not infer someone’s language, disability, cultural preference or interest from their name or their absence from a response list.

Accuracy, completeness and relevance to the intended purpose matter when assessing information. These counts are complete for the supplied practice exercise, yet incomplete for knowing every invitee’s reported understanding. Both can be true. Privately prepare a short statement with the respondent percentage, response coverage and distinct unknowns. The point is to help someone understand the finding on the first reading, not to produce the largest or smallest number available.

accordion.heading: Examine the question and its consequences

items.title: Explain the 66.7 percent finding
items.body: The denominator is eighteen respondents. This percentage describes their answers, not the thirty invitees’ complete experience. Felix can use it if he also explains how many invitees answered and keeps absent answers visible. It remains a useful finding without a false claim of full coverage or representativeness.

items.title: Keep the 40 percent description precise
items.body: Twelve recorded affirmative responses among thirty invitees is 40 percent. The arithmetic does not tell whether the other eighteen could identify a step. Six stated uncertainty; twelve gave no supplied answer. Zora can report the recorded share while refusing to convert these different statuses into a universal failure rate. The question about everyone’s understanding remains unresolved.

items.title: Consider access without pretending to know the cause
items.body: An actual evaluation might ask whether its invitation and participation routes fit people’s circumstances. Nonresponse makes that question worth considering; it does not answer it. Adding a channel, changing a deadline or collecting personal details requires a fitting reason and appropriate responsibility. No particular change, delivery defect, demographic cause or new information permission is supplied here.

tabs.heading: Compare the interpretation and next inquiry

tabs.label: Only the largest percentage is shown
tabs.body: Felix presents 66.7 percent without identifying respondents or response coverage. The calculation is correct, but readers cannot see the twelve absent answers. Zora adds twelve of eighteen respondents and eighteen of thirty invitees, with uncertain and absent answers distinguished. The finding becomes easier to understand without changing any response.

tabs.label: Unknown becomes failure
tabs.body: Zora initially calls the remaining eighteen invitees unsuccessful because only twelve affirmed. Felix separates six uncertain answers from twelve unknown answers. The forty-percent recorded share can be retained with an exact description, but it cannot establish eighteen failures. The revised account improves interpretation rather than inventing additional responses.

tabs.label: Counts and purposes stay together
tabs.body: Felix reports twelve of eighteen respondents affirmed, approximately 66.7 percent; eighteen of thirty invitees responded, 60 percent. Zora adds that six respondents were uncertain and twelve invitees’ answers are unknown. This compact account lets readers see the finding and its limits. It claims neither a representative sample nor completed action.

check.question: Which statement preserves the supplied response statuses?
check.correct: Twelve of eighteen respondents affirmed, approximately 66.7 percent; eighteen of thirty invitees answered, 60 percent, with six uncertain responses and twelve absent answers.
wrong: The 40 percent recorded affirmative share proves eighteen invitees failed.
The 60 percent response coverage is the demonstration’s understanding score.
The respondent percentage proves the absent invitees would answer the same way.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. The respondent finding, invitation coverage and different unanswered or uncertain conditions remain visible.
check.feedbackIncorrect: The other eighteen comprise six uncertain responses and twelve unknown answers, not eighteen verified failures. Response coverage describes answering the invitation, not identifying a next step. No evidence establishes how the absent invitees would answer.

sorting.heading: Keep findings, questions and conclusions distinct

items.text: Twelve affirmative answers among eighteen responses is approximately 66.7 percent.
Eighteen of thirty invitations received responses, 60 percent.
How would the twelve nonrespondents answer?
Why did an invitee not respond?
All eighteen without an affirmative answer failed.
A new response channel would automatically remove selection differences.

lessons.next: Continue to compare conditions without inventing a cause.

scenario.context: This example: Zora is deciding how to summarize twelve affirmative and six uncertain answers among eighteen responses from thirty invitees.
options: Call forty percent the success rate and all remaining invitees unsuccessful.
Report the affirmative respondent count and percentage beside invitation coverage, with uncertain and absent answers distinct.
Use sixty percent as proof of understanding and omit the unanswered invitations.
responses: This turns unknowns and uncertainty into failure without evidence.
This makes the finding understandable while retaining the twelve unanswered invitations and six uncertain responses.
Response coverage is not an understanding measure, and omitting absent answers hides a limit.

lessons.transfer: Privately calculate the three percentages and write the exact question each answers, keeping uncertain and absent answers distinct.

move.control: You can report a percentage beside its denominator, purpose and response coverage.
move.failure: A convenient number turns nonresponse into failure, understanding or representativeness.
move.next: Privately calculate the three percentages and write the exact question each answers, keeping uncertain and absent answers distinct.

lessons.title: Compare conditions without inventing a cause
lessons.summary: A separate hypothetical comparison can reveal a descriptive gap while leaving selection, context and causes open.
lessons.objective: Calculate the levels and percentage-point gap in the separate practice comparison.
objectives: Calculate the levels and percentage-point gap in the separate practice comparison.
Distinguish a descriptive comparison from an estimate of a demonstration’s causal effect.
Identify evidence and design questions that would matter to a stronger causal inquiry.
takeaways: A difference can be important without establishing its cause.
Self-selection and earlier conditions can affect comparisons.
A stronger question needs fitting evidence and design rather than a stronger headline.
lessons.statement: Describe the difference that is supplied, then separate it from explanations that have not been established.

image.caption: Four people lean toward one another and stack their hands above a table with papers, cups and laptops.

intro.heading: Compare conditions without inventing a cause
intro.body:
Zora and Felix consider a separate hypothetical illustration. It is not a continuation of the thirty-invitee survey or a later observation. In this comparison, fifteen of twenty people in an invented demonstration-attendee set report being able to identify a next step. Ten of twenty people in an invented nonattendee set report the same. Each person is counted once in their own set. The twenty-person sets are learning illustrations, not actual staff groups, assigned conditions or demographic categories.

Fifteen of twenty is 75 percent; ten of twenty is 50 percent. The descriptive difference is twenty-five percentage points. That is a comparison between percentages, not a finding that the demonstration caused twenty-five percent improvement. The illustration supplies no earlier understanding measure, random assignment, matching procedure or reason people attended. It also supplies no evidence that the two sets had comparable circumstances. People who chose to attend might have differed in prior interest, experience, available time or another unmeasured condition. Those are possible questions, not established explanations.

Felix suggests that the larger attendee percentage is enough to approve expansion. Zora separates the comparison from that decision. The supplied difference might support a question about the demonstration’s contribution, but it does not isolate that contribution. Approval for a real expansion would involve appropriate evidence, affected perspectives, resources and actual responsible decisions. The course provides no funding rule, cutoff, implementation authority or presumption that a statistically described difference justifies every next action.

Zora also resists a different error: dismissing the figures because they cannot prove cause. The two reported levels are still descriptive information for the hypothetical question. They can prompt examination of what the demonstration involved and how the sets were formed. A more appropriate inquiry might include earlier conditions, comparable participation opportunities and relevant alternative explanations. The actual design should fit the question and practical context, with someone competent to assess the methods and their limits. No single design is mandated for every DHS activity.

The comparison is about reported next-step understanding, not observed application. Even a better-supported effect on reported understanding would not automatically establish lasting service improvement, reduced systemic disparities or changed employee experience. Each wider claim needs its own appropriate evidence. A gap between these invented participation sets is not a definition of a protected-class disparity or a reason to infer identities from names. Equity considerations may shape which effects, perspectives and barriers deserve examination; they do not make any unexplained numerical difference a proven cause.

Privately write two sentences. First, describe the supplied levels and twenty-five-percentage-point difference. Second, explain that the illustration does not establish the cause or a later service result. Then identify one design question that could make an actual inquiry more informative. The worthwhile result is a disciplined comparison that helps determine what to ask next, rather than either a causal claim built from a gap or the abandonment of every limited finding.

flashcards.back: Fifteen of twenty is 75 percent; ten of twenty is 50 percent in the separate illustration.
Seventy-five minus fifty is twenty-five percentage points.
A claim that a particular change produced a result, which this comparison alone does not establish.
A possible difference related to who participates; no particular selection explanation is supplied here.
What existed before the activity; no earlier understanding measures are provided.
Actual authority to consider resources and action, not supplied by learning arithmetic.

accordion.heading: Examine the question and its consequences

items.title: Keep the illustration separate
items.body: The twenty-person comparison sets do not add to the earlier thirty-invitee survey. They are a new hypothetical illustration of comparison limits. Combining the figures would invent participants and a larger observed inquiry. Felix can state their separate status and calculate the supplied rates without turning them into later program results.

items.title: Ask how the groups came to differ
items.body: The illustration does not establish why people attended, what they already understood or whether the conditions were comparable. Those gaps matter to a causal claim. Zora can ask about the design and alternative explanations without announcing that self-selection definitely caused the difference. A methodological question is not itself the answer to the original question.

items.title: Keep inquiry and action connected responsibly
items.body: A descriptive difference can inform a decision discussion without deciding it. Expanding an actual activity would require an appropriate rationale, relevant evidence, resources and responsible roles. A hypothetical gap provides none of those commitments. The next step is a supported question for consideration, not an invented funding threshold, guaranteed benefit or direction to another person’s work.

tabs.heading: Compare the interpretation and next inquiry

tabs.label: The gap becomes proof of impact
tabs.body: Felix describes the twenty-five-point difference as the demonstration’s causal effect. The example describes neither earlier measures nor a design that isolates the contribution. Zora states the rates and gap as descriptive and asks about selection and comparable conditions. The comparison remains useful without an unearned causal conclusion.

tabs.label: Uncertainty erases every finding
tabs.body: Zora initially wants to discard the comparison because its cause is unknown. Felix retains the two supplied levels and their descriptive difference while naming the missing design information. The figures can motivate a better question. Their limited purpose does not turn them into proof of impact, and their limits do not make the arithmetic meaningless.

tabs.label: The next inquiry has a reason
tabs.body: Felix writes that the attendee set’s reported level is higher in this hypothetical illustration, with a twenty-five-point gap and no established cause. Zora asks what earlier conditions and participation differences an actual inquiry would need to consider. No new data, design approval, expansion or later result is supplied. The proposal improves the question rather than promising an answer.

check.question: What does the separate comparison establish?
check.correct: Reported levels of 75 and 50 percent, a descriptive twenty-five-percentage-point gap, with causes and wider effects unestablished.
wrong: A twenty-five-percentage-point causal improvement from attending the demonstration.
Proof that the twenty-person sets had equal prior understanding.
Automatic authority to expand the activity and commit its resources.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. The levels and descriptive difference are supported; cause, comparable prior conditions and actual action remain open.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A gap alone does not isolate the demonstration’s contribution. No earlier understanding measures or equal-condition design are supplied. A practice comparison creates no operating or funding authority.

sorting.heading: Keep findings, questions and conclusions distinct

items.text: Fifteen of twenty is 75 percent.
Seventy-five minus fifty is twenty-five percentage points.
How were the two participation sets formed?
What did each set understand before the demonstration?
The demonstration caused the whole gap.
This gap guarantees lasting service improvement.

lessons.next: Continue to consider whose meaning of a useful result is present.

scenario.context: Separate hypothetical illustration: reported next-step understanding is fifteen of twenty in an attendee set and ten of twenty in a nonattendee set. Earlier conditions and participation decisions are not supplied.
options: Declare the demonstration the proven cause and approve expansion.
Discard the levels because they cannot settle the cause.
Retain the descriptive levels and gap, name the causal limits and propose a fitting design question for actual consideration.
responses: Neither cause nor expansion authority is established.
Limited descriptive information can still support a useful next question.
This keeps the comparison useful without fabricating causal evidence or actual approval.

lessons.transfer: Privately describe the two levels, their descriptive gap and one design question that would matter before claiming cause.

move.control: You can explain a descriptive gap and the limits of a causal interpretation.
move.failure: A numerical difference becomes proof of impact, demographic cause or automatic authority.
move.next: Privately describe the two levels, their descriptive gap and one design question that would matter before claiming cause.

lessons.title: Consider whose meaning of a useful result is present
lessons.summary: Personally offered perspectives can widen a narrow outcome question without becoming group rules or substitute evidence.
lessons.objective: Identify the different personally offered meanings of a worthwhile result in the another example.
objectives: Identify the different personally offered meanings of a worthwhile result in the another example.
Explain how those meanings widen an initial judgment without assigning fixed cultural traits.
Revise an invitation so people can discuss a useful result without supplying a biography or accepting one definition.
takeaways: People may bring different personally learned meanings to a question about results.
A supplied perspective can inform a question without proving everyone shares it.
Understanding a meaning does not by itself establish that an activity produced it.
lessons.statement: Ask what a useful result means in this context while keeping personal perspectives and outcome evidence distinct.

image.caption: Four people lean toward one another and stack their hands above a table with papers, cups and laptops.

intro.heading: Consider whose meaning of a useful result is present
intro.body:
In a separate practice community learning circle, Willa asks what would make an upcoming shared activity worthwhile. She first proposes counting completed entries on a display. Reed says that, in a neighborhood walking circle he chose to join, a place became meaningful when a story connected it to other places and people. An isolated entry could be accurate yet leave that connection invisible. Celia says that, in an instrument-repair circle she chose to join, an early result mattered when someone could use a repaired part for a particular purpose, even while the larger restoration remained unfinished. These are personally offered accounts, not statements about an ethnic, religious, disability or other identity group.

Willa initially hears Reed as avoiding a measurable result and Celia as settling for incomplete work. Each account gives her reason to reconsider. Reed is describing connections that help an entry make sense within a larger whole. Celia is describing a usable change for a chosen purpose before every aspect of a project is complete. Neither says accuracy or sustained effort is unimportant. Willa’s first count has left out what these participants mean by worthwhile. Hearing those meanings makes the question broader and more relevant without showing that any particular activity has already delivered them.

The accounts are culturally learned in the ordinary sense of meaning shaped through participation and experience. The case does not identify the speakers’ demographic backgrounds, require them to speak for a community or rank their development. A person can draw on several experiences and change a view. Willa should not turn the walking-circle account into a rule that Reed always prefers a narrative, or the repair-circle account into a rule that Celia always wants a practical task. Their offered meanings belong to this encounter and can be explored through a question rather than converted into a script.

Willa revises her invitation: people may identify a meaningful connection, a usable change or another result that would make the activity worthwhile, and explain what could show that result in the context they choose. Someone may use a practice example, ask a question or keep a personal account private. A completed entry can still matter, but it is no longer the only permitted definition of value. The invitation supplies no requirement for biography, public reflection, immediate agreement or a shared numerical score. The exercise does not report that everyone accepted it or that the activity occurred.

Return carefully to Zora and Felix’s evaluation. The learning-circle encounter cannot explain the demonstration’s uncertain or absent answers. It shows why an evaluator may need to examine whose meaning is present in the question and whose is missing. People affected by actual work can help consider whether identifying a next step captures what matters and what further question is appropriate. Their perspectives inform the inquiry; they do not replace credible evidence of action or effects. Nor must every learner disclose a story for the evaluation to be legitimate.

Private reflection is a complete learning choice. Notice one meaning you initially left out and describe how it could change your next question. You can leave the encounter unresolved. Growth here involves a more context-sensitive interpretation and response, not a personnel rating, proof of an IDI orientation or a claim that a discussion itself established a program result.

accordion.heading: Examine the question and its consequences

items.title: Widen the first interpretation
items.body: Reed’s account gives Willa a meaning for connections that her completed-entry count did not capture. Celia’s gives a meaning for useful progress before whole-project completion. Willa can understand both without agreeing that either fits every activity. The consequence is a more suitable question about value, rather than a diagnosis of avoidance, a stereotype or a promise that every desired result is already present.

items.title: Keep the offered account personal
items.body: The example describes chosen participation in two circles, not demographic identities or rules about whole communities. Willa can ask how the meaning matters here while leaving room for other experiences. Requiring a biography, inferring a preferred learning style or treating one speaker as a representative would exceed the offered evidence and narrow the encounter instead of opening it.

items.title: Change the invitation and retain evidence
items.body: The revised invitation welcomes a meaningful connection, usable change or another fitting result. It does not require a story or declare the activity effective. If an actual evaluation adopted a relevant question, it would still need suitable evidence of what occurred. A better question and an observed beneficial result are different accomplishments; only the changed invitation is supplied in this encounter.

tabs.heading: Compare the interpretation and next inquiry

tabs.label: The account becomes a group script
tabs.body: Willa decides Reed must always want a story and Celia must always want a task. Their offered meanings concern chosen experiences and this particular discussion. A more thoughtful response asks what matters here and allows another answer. The cultural learning is the widened interpretation, not a fixed classification of either person.

tabs.label: Recognition becomes proof of impact
tabs.body: Willa says that because she now understands the accounts, the shared activity has produced meaningful results. The activity has not yet happened in the example. Reed’s and Celia’s meanings can help shape a question, but they provide no result data. Retaining that distinction respects their perspectives without asking them to certify a benefit.

tabs.label: A more flexible question stays honest
tabs.body: Willa invites a meaningful connection, usable change or another fitting result, using a personal or practice example or a question. The entry count remains an option rather than the whole definition. Acceptance and later outcomes remain open. intro.heading: Protect people and retain actual responsibilities
intro.body:
Felix wants to understand the demonstration’s unanswered invitations. He suggests connecting the response list to personnel records and publishing a breakdown. Zora recognizes a worthwhile question about participation, but the practice exercise provides no actual records, access permission or approved collection and disclosure arrangement. A question can be useful while a proposed method needs further consideration. The desire for a fuller evaluation does not itself authorize access, linkage, new demographic fields or public release.

In actual work, information about people must be handled through the applicable purpose, classification, access and security arrangements. Minnesota Statutes section 13.05 includes requirements concerning necessary collection and storage, permitted uses and accuracy and safeguards for individual data. This lesson does not determine every classification or authorize a particular use. Removing names does not automatically make a record anonymous, and combining a few responses does not automatically establish safe release. Context and other information can matter. The course creates no universal small-count threshold, pooling rule or retention period.

Affected people’s perspectives can help examine whether the inquiry’s question and participation choices fit. Their involvement should have a clear purpose and an accurate account of what participation entails. The American Evaluation Association’s guiding principles emphasize ethical conduct, respect, transparent limits and attention to the context of the work. Those principles are professional guidance, not a replacement for DHS policies, actual data responsibilities or a fixed survey method. A learning reflection also never becomes an employee record or a personal intercultural score.

A separate example concerns supervisor Alden, who receives a disability-related harassment allegation while a team is reviewing a learning activity. The evaluation schedule does not postpone the existing duty. Under MMB Policy 1436, managers and supervisors immediately report all protected-class harassment or discrimination allegations or incidents to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer and follow applicable agency procedures or the Affirmative Action Plan. Alden does not wait for a finished survey, proof, consensus, an apology, course completion or a consultant response. Assigned investigation and nonretaliation remain part of the actual process. This allegation example is distinct from the unexplained survey answers; an absent response is not itself the supplied allegation.

The Equity and Inclusion Operations Consultant leads the program and provides guidance, knowledge and feedback while staff carry their own equity work. Consultation can help sharpen a question, consider an interpretation or examine a proposed next action. It is not a mandatory approval gate for every resource use, and it does not make the consultant the person who collects every answer or completes staff’s work. Daily equity considerations and qualifying formal analyses retain their actual tools and responsibilities. A practice evaluation also gives no authority to change services, eligibility, staffing, expenditures or assigned decision roles.

Privately distinguish three things: a worthwhile question, a method that needs appropriate consideration and an existing duty that must continue. You can use the example without obtaining a real person’s record or account. Native American- and Tribal-specific matters remain referred to the person or area responsible within ADSA; this course does not independently teach those subjects or invent an office contact. These boundaries make room for responsible learning and analysis rather than treating uncertainty as permission or postponing obligations until an evaluation is complete.

items.title: Separate the question from the proposed method
items.body: Felix’s question about participation may be worth examining. Linking a response list to personnel records is a different decision requiring actual purpose and information arrangements. items.title: Do not make a learning count a privacy certificate
items.body: A report might omit names or show combined figures and still require careful review of actual disclosure conditions. The lesson supplies no universal threshold or determination that a particular release is safe. items.title: Retain immediate duties through the inquiry
items.body: Supervisor Alden’s supplied disability-related allegation triggers the actual reporting duty regardless of the evaluation’s progress. A completed report, private resolution or consultant response is not a condition. All protected-class allegations or incidents are immediately reported through HR or agency AAO and applicable agency procedures or the Affirmative Action Plan, with assigned investigation and nonretaliation preserved. The survey’s unexplained responses are a separate matter.

lessons.title: Turn the findings into a supported next question
lessons.summary: A recommendation can improve the inquiry and its usefulness without pretending that approval, action or later benefit has occurred.

lessons.statement: Recommend the next useful inquiry and make clear what has and has not happened.

intro.heading: Turn the findings into a supported next question
intro.body:
Zora and Felix return to the supplied demonstration survey. Their final account says twelve of eighteen respondents, approximately 66.7 percent, selected that they could identify a next step. Eighteen of thirty invitees answered, 60 percent. Six respondents were not yet sure which action fit, and twelve invitees’ answers were absent. The recorded affirmative share of the invitation set is twelve of thirty, 40 percent, if that specific description is needed. None of these figures measures correct application, later service improvement or the whole program’s effectiveness.

Felix now recommends considering a clearer inquiry into what remained uncertain and whether the question and participation routes fit the purpose. His recommendation has a reason: the supplied answers and coverage leave important questions open. It does not claim that the demonstration’s language caused uncertainty, that email caused nonresponse or that adding a new response channel would solve every problem. Actual materials are not supplied for inspection. Any review of the demonstration’s content or a proposed alternative method would need the relevant material, perspectives, evidence and appropriate responsibilities.

Zora helps keep the possible next inquiry focused. An actual plan could explain its purpose, the people it appropriately seeks to include, the question, how participation would work and the information arrangements. It could consider what evidence would make the answer useful and what effects or missing perspectives should be kept visible. The professional guidance emphasizes context, credible evidence, understandable limits and use of learning. It does not impose a universal deadline, retention duration or required survey for every activity. A proposal can identify an unanswered design choice rather than invent an approved procedure.

Their closing recommendation separates three stages. First is the supported description of the supplied responses. Second is the proposed inquiry into uncertainty and participation fit. Third would be any actual action and later evidence about its effects, neither of which is supplied. A revised question or explanation can be genuine progress in the quality of the work, while program outcomes remain unknown. No new response, completed collection, approved expenditure, scheduled review or beneficial service result is created by the recommendation.

The separate twenty-person comparison remains a hypothetical example of causal limits, not a later test of the proposal. Willa’s learning-circle invitation remains a distinct personal-meaning example, not the cause of uncertain survey answers. Alden’s immediate reporting duty remains an actual policy example, not a numerical finding from the survey. Keeping these encounters separate helps readers use the connected ideas without constructing a larger sample evidence base from unrelated learning illustrations.

Privately write a short conclusion, its limits and one justified next question. You may decide that a recommendation needs more information before it can responsibly propose a method. That is meaningful analytical work. Staff develop and carry their equity work while the Equity and Inclusion Operations Consultant leads the program and provides guidance, knowledge and feedback. The result of the course is a more faithful evaluation argument or private reflection, not a required public artifact or a claim that the program has already improved.

accordion.heading: Examine the question and its consequences

items.title: Connect the recommendation to the known limit
items.body: Six uncertain answers and twelve absent answers support questions about what remains unclear and whose experience is included. They do not establish why those conditions occurred. Felix’s recommendation can explain that reason and identify the evidence needed to consider a fitting inquiry. A reasoned question is stronger than prescribing a fix for a cause that has not been established.

items.title: Keep the proposal’s choices explicit
items.body: An actual inquiry would need an appropriate purpose, question, participation approach, information arrangements and responsible roles. The course can identify these as considerations without deciding them for every program. Zora can leave a method open when material or authority is missing. No universal survey, Friday deadline, new fields, retention period or funding promise follows from the exercise.

items.title: Name progress without inventing an outcome
items.body: The pair’s account is clearer because it keeps findings, uncertainty and recommendations separate. That change is supplied. No later action or benefit is supplied. A future evaluation would need actual observations and fitting comparisons before reporting an effect. Unknown later results are unknown; they are neither success nor a reason to announce no warning signs.

tabs.heading: Compare the interpretation and next inquiry

tabs.label: The recommendation promises a fix
tabs.body: Felix initially writes that a new survey channel will remove the uncertainty and prove the program works. No cause or later result supports that promise. Zora suggests considering how people could participate when the team investigates that question. The recommendation becomes usable because its rationale and unresolved choices are visible.

tabs.label: Different illustrations become one study
tabs.body: Zora combines the thirty-invitee survey with the separate twenty-person sets and the learning-circle discussion. They were not supplied as connected participants or observations. Felix separates each illustration and its purpose. The concepts can inform one another while the evidence cannot be merged into a larger invented study or later outcome.

tabs.label: A clear next question retains honest status
tabs.body: Felix describes the responses and coverage, recommends examining uncertain understanding and participation fit, and identifies the material and responsibilities needed to consider a method. Zora accepts that formulation for the proposal. The revised account is the supplied progress. Actual approval, collection, changed activity and later benefits remain unestablished.

sections.heading: Define the purpose and people included
items: Zora and Felix’s original practice demonstration inquiry concerns reported next-step understanding. The actual demonstration materials are not supplied; no review of those materials, observed application or whole-program effectiveness is claimed.

Thirty unique invented attendees were invited once by email after one demonstration, and eighteen answered once. The invitation set does not describe all staff or people who did not attend or receive the invitation. Their experiences and counts are not supplied.

A fitting actual evaluation question needs relevant context and perspectives, suitable evidence and appropriate responsibilities. The learning exercise does not impose one survey or denominator on every program.

sections.heading: Explain each response figure
items: Twelve of eighteen respondents selected that they could identify a next step: approximately 66.7 percent among respondents. Six of the eighteen said they were not yet sure which action fit.

Eighteen of thirty invitees answered, 60 percent response coverage. Twelve invitees have no supplied answer, and their understanding and reasons are unknown. Coverage is not an understanding score or proof of representativeness.

Twelve recorded affirmative responses among thirty invitees is 40 percent. If used, describe it as the recorded affirmative share of the invitation set, not a success rate or proof that the other eighteen failed. Six uncertain responses and twelve absent answers are not interchangeable.

No response status establishes effort, language, disability, cultural preference or an IDI orientation. An additional participation route may be considered appropriately; it does not automatically remove selection differences or prove a cause.

sections.heading: Read the separate comparison without a causal claim
items: The separate hypothetical illustration has fifteen of twenty in an attendee set reporting next-step understanding, 75 percent, and ten of twenty in a nonattendee set, 50 percent. Each person is counted once in their set. These are not later responses from the thirty-invitee survey or demographic categories.

The descriptive gap is twenty-five percentage points. No earlier measures, random assignment, matching or participation reasons are supplied. The gap does not isolate the demonstration’s contribution or establish a particular selection explanation.

Keep the descriptive comparison and ask about suitable design and alternative explanations. No causal effect, lasting service benefit, funding threshold, expansion approval or operating authority is established.

sections.heading: Hear personally offered meanings of a useful result
items: In the separate learning-circle encounter, Reed describes a place making sense through connected stories in a chosen walking circle. Celia describes a repaired part becoming useful for a particular purpose before a larger instrument restoration ends. Their selected experiences supply no demographic group rules.

Willa’s initial judgments of avoiding measurement and accepting incomplete work widen. She invites a meaningful connection, usable change or another fitting result, with a personal or practice example or a question. A completed entry remains an option rather than the only definition of value.

The invitation requires no biography, public reflection or agreement. Acceptance and later activity results are not supplied. The encounter cannot explain the demonstration’s uncertain or absent answers or establish a personal developmental rank.
Affected perspectives can help examine whether an actual question captures what matters. They inform inquiry without replacing evidence of what occurred or making disclosure compulsory.

sections.heading: Preserve actual information and reporting responsibilities
items: A question about unanswered invitations does not authorize access to personnel records, linkage, new fields or public disclosure. Actual purpose, classification, access and security arrangements remain. Removing names or combining small counts is not an automatic privacy certificate.

Professional evaluation principles guide ethical reasoning; they do not replace DHS policies or supply a universal method or retention period. Daily equity considerations and qualifying formal analyses keep their actual tools and roles.

In the separate example, supervisor Alden immediately reports all protected-class harassment or discrimination allegations or incidents to HR or agency AAO and follows applicable agency procedures or the Affirmative Action Plan. Proof, a finished evaluation, consensus, apology, course completion or consultant response is not a reporting condition. Assigned investigation and nonretaliation remain.
The allegation example is distinct from unexplained survey answers. Native American- and Tribal-specific matters remain referred to the person or area responsible within ADSA; no contact is invented.

sections.heading: Return a supported finding and next question
items: State the respondent result and invitation coverage with uncertain and absent answers visible. Zora and Felix’s final proposal considers an inquiry into uncertainty and participation fit because those questions remain open, without claiming a known cause.

An actual method would need relevant material, perspectives, purpose, information arrangements and responsible decisions. The recommendation provides no universal schedule, survey, new collection, resource commitment or approved procedure.

The clearer account and proposal are the supplied progress. Actual approval, collection, changed activity and later effects remain unestablished. Missing later results are unknown, not success or no warning signs. Keep the separate comparison, personal encounter and allegation example from becoming one invented study.

Staff carry their equity work while the consultant leads the program and offers guidance, knowledge and feedback; optional consultation does not create a universal review gate. Private reflection is legitimate without a live project or public artifact.
